transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve been having trouble keeping my focus at work. I’m a receptionist, so I’m scheduling appointments and answering questions, and sometimes I’ll be right in the middle of putting something in the calendar or working on the lobby displays, and I just… lose my place. Like my mind slips off to thinking about what I might have missed or overlooked, and then I have to backtrack and check what I was doing.

It’s not like I can’t do my job, exactly, but it’s been happening enough that it’s bothering me. I’ll be trying to concentrate, and then I’m mentally going through, “Did I forget to call someone back? Did I put that in the right spot? Did I miss a detail?” and then I realize I’ve stopped paying attention to the thing right in front of me. That’s really why I’m here.
Do you find yourself worrying about things more than you think you should?

Yes… I do. More than I think I should, honestly. It’s not always one huge thing, either — it’s all these ordinary things that somehow feel like they could go wrong if I don’t keep turning them over in my head.

Like at work, I’ll worry about the schedule, whether I put someone in the right slot or if I missed a note. Or with bills, even if they’re handled, I’ll still think, “What if I forgot one?” If I’m making travel plans, even something simple, I start going through every possible mix-up. And little paperwork errors — things that probably would be fixable — they feel like they could turn into some much bigger problem. I know, logically, that one small mistake usually isn’t the end of the world, but in the moment my mind treats it like it could snowball.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or muscle tension when you're worrying?

Yes, I think so — especially tension. I don’t always notice it right away because I’m still doing my job, you know, smiling at people at the front desk, answering the phone, trying to sound calm and pleasant. But inside I feel really wound tight, like I’m bracing for something to go wrong.

A lot of the time my shoulders are up around my ears without me realizing it. Then at some point I’ll catch myself and try to drop them, but they just creep right back up. It’s like my body is waiting for the next mistake or problem, even if nothing is actually happening in that moment.
Have you ever had a sudden feeling of intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, like a sudden wave that comes out of nowhere and peaks really fast. I mean, I can feel very uncomfortable when I’m worrying, and sometimes it builds up and I’ll realize I’m really tense or on edge, but it’s more like it keeps running in the background and ramps up depending on what I’m thinking about.

I wouldn’t say I’ve had those moments where it’s like, all at once, “Something terrible is happening right now,” and then it peaks within minutes. At least, not that I can clearly point to. Mine feels more drawn out, like I get stuck in the worrying and checking and replaying things, rather than a sudden intense fear spell.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain tasks or situations because of your worrying?

I’m not sure I’d say I avoid things exactly… not in a really obvious way, anyway. I still go to work, I still answer the phones, deal with people at the front desk, handle paperwork — I don’t just refuse to do things because I’m worried.

But I guess sometimes I’ll put things off a little if I’m worried I’m going to mess them up, like I’ll want to check details first or wait until I feel like I have enough time to do it carefully. It’s more that I slow myself down than completely avoid it. I might keep rereading something or double-checking before I send it or turn it in, because I don’t want to create a problem for someone else.

So… I don’t think I’m avoiding whole situations, no. It’s more like I get caught up in making sure I’ve done things right, and that can make me hesitate.
Do you ever find yourself repeating certain actions or thoughts over and over, even when you don't want to?

Yes… but it’s more in my head than like doing some obvious ritual, if that makes sense. I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled. You already checked it,” or, “You already answered that question,” and for a second I believe it. But then the thought comes right back around.

Like I’ll start with one thing — did I give the right information, did I word that message clearly, did I forget some little detail — and then before I know it, I’ve moved on to three other concerns. It kind of loops. I’ll be checking details in my head over and over, almost like I’m trying to prove to myself that everything is okay, but it doesn’t really settle me for long.

I don’t always want to be doing it. Actually, most of the time I’m tired of it. I’ll think, “Just stop, it’s fine,” but my mind keeps going back through it anyway.
Do you feel compelled to perform specific acts, like checking or counting, in response to your worries?

I don’t think I feel compelled in that way, no. I mean, I do check things sometimes, but it doesn’t feel like a very specific act I have to do a certain number of times or anything like counting or touching things or following a rule.

It’s more ordinary checking, I guess — like if I’m unsure whether I wrote something down correctly, I might look again, or if I’m worried I misunderstood something, I might review it. But I wouldn’t say I have a set routine where I think, “I have to do this or something bad will happen.” It’s more that I’m trying to reassure myself that I didn’t miss something.

So… no counting. No specific ritual that I can think of. Just a lot of going back over things when I’m uncertain.
Are your worries usually about one specific type of thing or are they spread across many different areas of your life?

They’re definitely spread out. It’s not just one thing, like only money or only work. It can be all kinds of ordinary stuff, and that’s part of what makes it frustrating, because sometimes I’ll think, “Why am I turning this into such a big deal?”

At work it might be the schedule, or whether I gave someone the right information, or if a little paperwork mistake is going to cause trouble later. Then at home it might be bills, or making sure a travel plan is right, or whether I forgot some small detail that’s going to snowball into something bigger.

It’s usually not dramatic things, either. It’s everyday things. But in my head it’s like one small mix-up could turn into a whole chain of problems, and then I start trying to think through every possible way it could go wrong.
Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your overall quality of life or relationships with others?

Yeah… I mean, I’m still functioning. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m falling apart or not able to do my job, because I do show up, I get through the day, I answer people, I do what I’m supposed to do.

But it does interfere, just in these smaller ways that add up. Like scheduling takes me longer than it should now because I keep double-checking myself. I’ll look at an appointment or a calendar entry and think, “Okay, that’s right,” and then a minute later I’m back checking the same thing again because I don’t trust that I didn’t miss something. So what should be quick ends up taking extra time, and then I feel behind or embarrassed, even if nobody else notices right away.

And there have been times with the lobby displays where I’m arranging things, and because I’m so in my head or going back over details, I lose track of what I was doing. Then I have to redo parts of it because I realize it doesn’t look right or I forgot what order I was putting things in. It’s not huge, but it’s frustrating. It makes the day feel harder than it needs to be.
Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

Yes, that happens a lot. It’s not usually like one strange thought out of nowhere, it’s more like a concern gets stuck and keeps circling back even after I’ve already dealt with it.

I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled. You checked it. You wrote it down. It’s fine.” And for maybe a moment I’ll believe that, but then the thought comes right back, like, “But what if you wrote the wrong time?” or “What if you misunderstood what they said?” Then I start replaying the details in my head again, almost like I’m reviewing a little mental checklist, even when I’m trying to move on.

And the annoying part is it doesn’t always stay on the first thing. It’ll jump. So I’ll start with one worry, like an appointment time, and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I gave someone the right information, and then whether I forgot something else, and before I know it I’ve gone from one concern to another and I’m checking the same details in my head over and over.

I can usually keep doing what I need to do, but it feels like there’s this extra track running in the background that I can’t quite shut off.
Do you often feel restless or on edge, even when there's no apparent reason to be?

Yes, I do. It’s not always obvious from the outside, I don’t think. Like at the front desk, I can still smile and greet people and answer the phone and help them with whatever they need, so I probably look normal enough. But inside I feel really wound tight a lot of the time.

It’s like my body is bracing for something, even if nothing is actually happening right then. I’ll notice my shoulders are all tense, almost like they’re up around my ears, and I’m sitting there waiting for something to go wrong. Not even a specific thing necessarily, just this feeling like I need to be ready. And then if someone walks up suddenly or the phone rings, I’m already kind of on edge before I even know what they need.

So yes, I guess restless is the right word, but it’s more like tense and keyed up than pacing around or anything dramatic. I’m still doing my job and talking to people, but inside I feel like I can’t fully relax.
Do you avoid making decisions or taking actions because you're afraid of making a mistake?

Yes… I think I do, though it’s not always that I completely avoid the decision. It’s more that I hesitate, or I put it off, or I make it much bigger in my head than it probably needs to be.

Like with work schedules, I’ll worry that if I enter something wrong or misunderstand a time, it’s going to create this whole chain of problems for someone else. Or with bills, even ordinary ones, I’ll look at the amount or the due date and think, “What if I missed something?” Travel plans are the same way. I can get stuck checking times, addresses, confirmation numbers, because in my mind one little mix-up could turn into a whole mess.

And paperwork too, even small things. If there’s a tiny error or I’m not completely sure I wrote something correctly, I can feel myself freezing a bit before I move on, because I’m imagining it turning into a bigger problem later. So I still do things, usually, but it takes me longer because I’m trying so hard not to make a mistake.
Have you noticed your worrying affecting your relationships with friends or family?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think it’s caused any big fights or anything like that, at least not that I can clearly point to. My family and friends know I can be a little… careful, I guess, or that I like to double-check things, but I don’t know if they see it as a serious problem.

Sometimes I wonder if I ask for reassurance more than I realize, like, “Did I say that right?” or “Are you sure that’s the time?” But I’m not sure whether that actually bothers them or if I’m just assuming it might. People close to me are usually pretty patient, so it’s hard for me to tell.

So I guess my honest answer is, I haven’t really noticed a major impact on my relationships. Maybe small things here and there, but nothing obvious enough that someone has said, “This is affecting us,” if that makes sense.
Do you have thoughts that are intrusive or unwanted, and that you try to suppress or ignore?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, I have worries that pop into my head when I don’t want them to, like thinking over something I said or wondering if I forgot something, but I don’t know if that’s the same as an intrusive thought.

When you say intrusive or unwanted, I think of something that feels really strange or disturbing and I’m trying hard to push it away, and I don’t really think I have that. It’s more like regular worries that keep coming back, and I’ll try to distract myself or tell myself, “Okay, stop thinking about this,” but it’s not like I’m scared of the thought itself, if that makes sense.

So… I guess my answer is no, not in the way I think you mean. I haven’t really noticed specific thoughts that feel intrusive like that.
Do you often worry about everyday things, like chores or minor decisions, even when there's no obvious reason to be concerned?

Yes, I do. It’s honestly kind of embarrassing because the things are usually so ordinary. It’s not like there’s some obvious crisis happening, but my mind treats it like there could be one if I’m not careful enough.

Like with work schedules, I’ll start worrying that maybe I wrote down the wrong time, or misunderstood what someone told me, and then I picture it causing problems for other people. With bills, even if it’s just a normal bill I pay every month, I’ll find myself checking the due date or the amount and thinking, “What if I missed something?” Travel plans are probably another one — I can get caught up in whether the time is right, whether the address is right, whether I should recheck the confirmation.

And it can be really small paperwork things too. Like if I make a tiny error or I’m not completely sure something was filled out correctly, I worry it could turn into some bigger problem later. So yes, I worry about everyday things more than I think makes sense. It’s like one small mix-up feels like it could snowball, even when there isn’t really a clear reason to think that.
Do you have thoughts that feel like they're stuck in your head and you can't stop thinking about them, even when you want to?

Yes… I think that does happen, though it feels more like worry getting stuck than one specific thought. Like I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled,” or “You already checked that,” and for a second I’ll feel like, okay, I can move on. But then it comes right back around.

It’ll start with one thing, like whether I got a detail right, and then pretty soon it connects to something else, and then something else. I’ll be going over it in my head, almost like mentally checking a list over and over, even when I don’t really want to be doing that anymore.

It’s not constant every minute, but when it happens, it’s hard to just drop it. I know logically that I’ve probably already taken care of it, but my mind keeps looping back anyway, like it wants to be completely sure before it lets me relax.
Do you feel like your worrying is affecting your ability to enjoy your free time or pursue hobbies?

Yeah… somewhat. I wouldn’t say it’s completely stopping me from doing things, because I’m still showing up, still getting through the day, still doing what I need to do. But it does sort of eat into my time and my attention more than I want to admit.

Like at work, scheduling takes me longer than it used to because I keep double-checking myself. I’ll look at the time, then look again, then compare it to what I wrote somewhere else, and it’s not that I don’t know how to do it — I do — but I get worried I’ve missed something small. So something that should be quick ends up taking extra time.

And even with things that are supposed to be more enjoyable or creative, like arranging the lobby displays, I’ve had times where I lose track of what I was doing because I’m second-guessing a detail or thinking back over something else. Then I realize I’ve kind of messed up the arrangement or forgotten where I was, and I have to redo parts of it. It’s frustrating, because that kind of thing should feel satisfying, and instead I’m spending more time fixing it or checking it than enjoying it.

So… yes, it affects my free time and hobbies a little, mostly because I have less mental space left over. It’s not like I’m unable to function, but things take longer, and I don’t feel as relaxed as I think I should.
Do you worry about most areas of your life, such as work, finances, relationships, and health, or is it mainly focused on one or two areas?

It’s more than just one area, I think. It kind of spreads around to a lot of ordinary life stuff. Work is definitely one, especially schedules or whether I understood a detail correctly. But then it’s bills too, like whether I paid the right amount or got the due date right, even when it’s something routine.

And travel plans — even simple ones — I’ll worry about the time, the address, the confirmation, all of that. Paperwork is another big one, even small errors. I’ll think, “What if this tiny mistake turns into something bigger later?” So it’s not just, say, finances or just work. It’s more like my mind treats lots of normal things as if one small mix-up could snowball into a bigger problem.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress or interfering with your daily life in a significant way?

Yes… I mean, I’d say it’s interfering, but maybe not in a dramatic way. I’m still showing up. I’m still going to work, answering phones, helping people, doing the things I’m supposed to do. It’s not like I’m missing work or completely unable to function.

But it does slow me down more than it used to. Scheduling especially takes me longer now because I keep double-checking myself. I’ll enter something or write it down, and then I’ll go back and look again, sometimes more than once, because I get this feeling like maybe I copied the time wrong or missed some small detail. So a task that should be straightforward ends up taking up extra time and energy.

And with the lobby displays, which I usually like doing, I’ve had times where I lose track of what I was arranging because my mind is caught on some detail or I’m second-guessing something. Then I realize it doesn’t look right or I forgot where I was in the setup, and I have to redo parts of it. That feels frustrating, because I’m getting through the day, but it’s like everything takes more effort than it should. So… significant? Maybe mildly significant. Not ruining my life, but definitely making daily things harder.
Would you say that your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?

Yes… I mean, I wouldn’t say “a lot” like I’m falling apart or I can’t function, because I am still showing up and getting through the day. I go to work, I do what I’m supposed to do, I deal with people, all of that.

But it is distressing in this quieter, constant way. Like with scheduling, I know how to do it, but I’ll keep going back and checking what I wrote or entered because I get worried I missed something small. And then suddenly something simple has taken much longer than it should, and I feel irritated with myself.

And even the lobby displays — which I usually like doing — I’ve had moments where I lose track of what I was arranging because I’m stuck second-guessing something, and then I have to redo parts of it. So it’s not unbearable, but yes, it bothers me. It makes me feel like my day takes more effort than it should.

doctor.question: Do you have thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to stop thinking about them?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether thoughts keep repeating despite attempts to stop them, which directly matches difficulty controlling or stopping worry.

patient.answer:
Yes, that happens a lot. It’s not usually like one strange thought out of nowhere, it’s more like a concern gets stuck and keeps circling back even after I’ve already dealt with it.

I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled. You checked it. You wrote it down. It’s fine.” And for maybe a moment I’ll believe that, but then the thought comes right back, like, “But what if you wrote the wrong time?” or “What if you misunderstood what they said?” Then I start replaying the details in my head again, almost like I’m reviewing a little mental checklist, even when I’m trying to move on.

And the annoying part is it doesn’t always stay on the first thing. It’ll jump. So I’ll start with one worry, like an appointment time, and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I gave someone the right information, and then whether I forgot something else, and before I know it I’ve gone from one concern to another and I’m checking the same details in my head over and over.

I can usually keep doing what I need to do, but it feels like there’s this extra track running in the background that I can’t quite shut off.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of restlessness or feeling on edge
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless or on edge, even when there's no apparent reason to be?

target_item.name: Restlessness_Tension
target_item.manifestation: At the front desk I can still smile and help people, but inside I feel wound tight, like my shoulders are up around my ears and I’m waiting for something to go wrong.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling restless or on edge without an apparent reason, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. It’s not always obvious from the outside, I don’t think. Like at the front desk, I can still smile and greet people and answer the phone and help them with whatever they need, so I probably look normal enough. But inside I feel really wound tight a lot of the time.

It’s like my body is bracing for something, even if nothing is actually happening right then. I’ll notice my shoulders are all tense, almost like they’re up around my ears, and I’m sitting there waiting for something to go wrong. Not even a specific thing necessarily, just this feeling like I need to be ready. And then if someone walks up suddenly or the phone rings, I’m already kind of on edge before I even know what they need.

So yes, I guess restless is the right word, but it’s more like tense and keyed up than pacing around or anything dramatic. I’m still doing my job and talking to people, but inside I feel like I can’t fully relax.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance behaviors due to fear of making mistakes
doctor.question: Do you avoid making decisions or taking actions because you're afraid of making a mistake?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.
target_item.reason: The question is mainly about fear of making mistakes, which fits the profile of excessive worry about ordinary things like paperwork errors turning into bigger problems.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I do, though it’s not always that I completely avoid the decision. It’s more that I hesitate, or I put it off, or I make it much bigger in my head than it probably needs to be.

Like with work schedules, I’ll worry that if I enter something wrong or misunderstand a time, it’s going to create this whole chain of problems for someone else. Or with bills, even ordinary ones, I’ll look at the amount or the due date and think, “What if I missed something?” Travel plans are the same way. I can get stuck checking times, addresses, confirmation numbers, because in my mind one little mix-up could turn into a whole mess.

And paperwork too, even small things. If there’s a tiny error or I’m not completely sure I wrote something correctly, I can feel myself freezing a bit before I move on, because I’m imagining it turning into a bigger problem later. So I still do things, usually, but it takes me longer because I’m trying so hard not to make a mistake.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning due to worrying
doctor.question: Have you noticed your worrying affecting your relationships with friends or family?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about effects on relationships with friends or family, but the provided symptom profile only describes impairment at work and does not cover social or family relationship impact.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think it’s caused any big fights or anything like that, at least not that I can clearly point to. My family and friends know I can be a little… careful, I guess, or that I like to double-check things, but I don’t know if they see it as a serious problem.

Sometimes I wonder if I ask for reassurance more than I realize, like, “Did I say that right?” or “Are you sure that’s the time?” But I’m not sure whether that actually bothers them or if I’m just assuming it might. People close to me are usually pretty patient, so it’s hard for me to tell.

So I guess my honest answer is, I haven’t really noticed a major impact on my relationships. Maybe small things here and there, but nothing obvious enough that someone has said, “This is affecting us,” if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of obsessive thoughts
doctor.question: Do you have thoughts that are intrusive or unwanted, and that you try to suppress or ignore?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about intrusive, unwanted thoughts that are suppressed or ignored, which is more specific to obsessions; the provided symptom profile covers generalized worry but not intrusive obsessional thoughts.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, I have worries that pop into my head when I don’t want them to, like thinking over something I said or wondering if I forgot something, but I don’t know if that’s the same as an intrusive thought.

When you say intrusive or unwanted, I think of something that feels really strange or disturbing and I’m trying hard to push it away, and I don’t really think I have that. It’s more like regular worries that keep coming back, and I’ll try to distract myself or tell myself, “Okay, stop thinking about this,” but it’s not like I’m scared of the thought itself, if that makes sense.

So… I guess my answer is no, not in the way I think you mean. I haven’t really noticed specific thoughts that feel intrusive like that.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of excessive anxiety about everyday things
doctor.question: Do you often worry about everyday things, like chores or minor decisions, even when there's no obvious reason to be concerned?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about frequent worry over ordinary everyday matters without clear cause, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. It’s honestly kind of embarrassing because the things are usually so ordinary. It’s not like there’s some obvious crisis happening, but my mind treats it like there could be one if I’m not careful enough.

Like with work schedules, I’ll start worrying that maybe I wrote down the wrong time, or misunderstood what someone told me, and then I picture it causing problems for other people. With bills, even if it’s just a normal bill I pay every month, I’ll find myself checking the due date or the amount and thinking, “What if I missed something?” Travel plans are probably another one — I can get caught up in whether the time is right, whether the address is right, whether I should recheck the confirmation.

And it can be really small paperwork things too. Like if I make a tiny error or I’m not completely sure something was filled out correctly, I worry it could turn into some bigger problem later. So yes, I worry about everyday things more than I think makes sense. It’s like one small mix-up feels like it could snowball, even when there isn’t really a clear reason to think that.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of obsessive thoughts
doctor.question: Do you have thoughts that feel like they're stuck in your head and you can't stop thinking about them, even when you want to?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about being unable to stop thoughts or worries once they start, which directly matches difficulty controlling worry.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that does happen, though it feels more like worry getting stuck than one specific thought. Like I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled,” or “You already checked that,” and for a second I’ll feel like, okay, I can move on. But then it comes right back around.

It’ll start with one thing, like whether I got a detail right, and then pretty soon it connects to something else, and then something else. I’ll be going over it in my head, almost like mentally checking a list over and over, even when I don’t really want to be doing that anymore.

It’s not constant every minute, but when it happens, it’s hard to just drop it. I know logically that I’ve probably already taken care of it, but my mind keeps looping back anyway, like it wants to be completely sure before it lets me relax.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like your worrying is affecting your ability to enjoy your free time or pursue hobbies?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up and getting through the day, but scheduling takes me longer now because I double-check myself so much, and I’ve had to redo parts of the lobby displays after losing track of what I was arranging.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the worry is interfering with functioning and enjoyment of activities, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah… somewhat. I wouldn’t say it’s completely stopping me from doing things, because I’m still showing up, still getting through the day, still doing what I need to do. But it does sort of eat into my time and my attention more than I want to admit.

Like at work, scheduling takes me longer than it used to because I keep double-checking myself. I’ll look at the time, then look again, then compare it to what I wrote somewhere else, and it’s not that I don’t know how to do it — I do — but I get worried I’ve missed something small. So something that should be quick ends up taking extra time.

And even with things that are supposed to be more enjoyable or creative, like arranging the lobby displays, I’ve had times where I lose track of what I was doing because I’m second-guessing a detail or thinking back over something else. Then I realize I’ve kind of messed up the arrangement or forgotten where I was, and I have to redo parts of it. It’s frustrating, because that kind of thing should feel satisfying, and instead I’m spending more time fixing it or checking it than enjoying it.

So… yes, it affects my free time and hobbies a little, mostly because I have less mental space left over. It’s not like I’m unable to function, but things take longer, and I don’t feel as relaxed as I think I should.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's worrying is generalized and pervasive across different aspects of life
doctor.question: Do you worry about most areas of your life, such as work, finances, relationships, and health, or is it mainly focused on one or two areas?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the worry spans many areas of life rather than being limited to one or two, which directly matches excessive worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
It’s more than just one area, I think. It kind of spreads around to a lot of ordinary life stuff. Work is definitely one, especially schedules or whether I understood a detail correctly. But then it’s bills too, like whether I paid the right amount or got the due date right, even when it’s something routine.

And travel plans — even simple ones — I’ll worry about the time, the address, the confirmation, all of that. Paperwork is another big one, even small errors. I’ll think, “What if this tiny mistake turns into something bigger later?” So it’s not just, say, finances or just work. It’s more like my mind treats lots of normal things as if one small mix-up could snowball into a bigger problem.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant distress or impairment
doctor.question: Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress or interfering with your daily life in a significant way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up and getting through the day, but scheduling takes me longer now because I double-check myself so much, and I’ve had to redo parts of the lobby displays after losing track of what I was arranging.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry causes distress or significantly interferes with daily life, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, I’d say it’s interfering, but maybe not in a dramatic way. I’m still showing up. I’m still going to work, answering phones, helping people, doing the things I’m supposed to do. It’s not like I’m missing work or completely unable to function.

But it does slow me down more than it used to. Scheduling especially takes me longer now because I keep double-checking myself. I’ll enter something or write it down, and then I’ll go back and look again, sometimes more than once, because I get this feeling like maybe I copied the time wrong or missed some small detail. So a task that should be straightforward ends up taking up extra time and energy.

And with the lobby displays, which I usually like doing, I’ve had times where I lose track of what I was arranging because my mind is caught on some detail or I’m second-guessing something. Then I realize it doesn’t look right or I forgot where I was in the setup, and I have to redo parts of it. That feels frustrating, because I’m getting through the day, but it’s like everything takes more effort than it should. So… significant? Maybe mildly significant. Not ruining my life, but definitely making daily things harder.

doctor.question: Would you say that your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

Yes… I mean, I wouldn’t say “a lot” like I’m falling apart or I can’t function, because I am still showing up and getting through the day. I go to work, I do what I’m supposed to do, I deal with people, all of that.

But it is distressing in this quieter, constant way. Like with scheduling, I know how to do it, but I’ll keep going back and checking what I wrote or entered because I get worried I missed something small. And then suddenly something simple has taken much longer than it should, and I feel irritated with myself.

And even the lobby displays — which I usually like doing — I’ve had moments where I lose track of what I was arranging because I’m stuck second-guessing something, and then I have to redo parts of it. So it’s not unbearable, but yes, it bothers me. It makes me feel like my day takes more effort than it should.
